Home Publications INSS Insight Between Development and Oversight: China’s Approach to Addressing Artificial Intelligence Risks

The rapid development of artificial intelligence capabilities is broadening the way China defines the risks posed by this technology. Alongside espionage, cyber threats, and familiar national security threats, Beijing is increasingly addressing the risks originating from advanced AI systems themselves—including autonomous operation and loss of control. At the same time, technological lag and dependence on foreign technologies are also perceived as risks to national security. Official publications from September 2026 show that different approaches to these risks exist within the Chinese system, but all call for continued development of domestic AI capabilities alongside expanded mechanisms for safety, oversight, and control.

In mid-September 2026, Chinese officials issued three major statements on AI risks. On September 13, Minister of State Security Chen Yixin published an article addressing their implications for Chinese national security. The following day, the Artificial Intelligence Safety Governance Framework 3.0 was released, mapping the risks and the tools for addressing them. The Chinese Foreign Ministry also addressed AI risks and the possibility of slowing the development of advanced models.

This sequence of statements reflects different perspectives among China’s institutional bodies. Chen’s article examines the technology through the lens of national security, while Framework 3.0, developed by cybersecurity and standardization bodies, gives greater weight to risks arising from the systems’ evolving capabilities. The Foreign Ministry connects the two dimensions, presenting risk management as compatible with continued development. In any case, the boundaries between them are not clear-cut: the Chinese term anquan (安全) denotes both "safety" and "security," bringing technological safety, cybersecurity, political stability, and national security under a single conceptual framework.

Chen Yixin, Secretary of the Party Committee and Minister of State Security (MSS), published his article ahead of National Cybersecurity Awareness Week. It draws heavily on earlier ideas and formulations of the Chinese leadership. A comparative analysis by Mark Parker Young, a former CIA analyst and senior official at the US National Intelligence Council, found that a significant portion of the minister's language is based on earlier documents and statements by President Xi Jinping and other Chinese officials. However, the section on AI risks contains a high proportion of material that could not be traced to previous texts, suggesting that the innovation lies primarily in applying existing security concepts to recent developments in the field.

Chen outlines six types of risks stemming from the development of artificial intelligence. For the purposes of this analysis, they can be grouped into three spheres. The first is the political and social sphere, which includes threats to political and ideological security, as well as challenges to governance and social order. In this context, Chen warns against the use of deepfakes, AI-generated content, and automated accounts to spread disinformation, inflame disputes, and wage cognitive warfare against China. He also points to algorithmic bias, privacy violations, and the difficulty of establishing accountability for automated decisions.

The second sphere concerns cybersecurity, espionage, and information security. According to Chen, artificial intelligence lowers the cost and skill barrier for executing cyberattacks, enabling the discovery of vulnerabilities and the automation of attacks, and even “AI versus AI” confrontations. He further warns against foreign intelligence services using the technology to collect and analyze sensitive data, as well as data leakage to foreign AI products.

The third sphere is technological and military competition. Chen frames technological gaps and dependency as a risk, arguing that countries with an advantage in the field use technology restrictions, standards, and closed systems to limit other countries’ access to advanced technologies. At the same time, he points to the increasing integration of AI in intelligence, decision-making, target identification, operational support, and cognitive influence. He describes a shift of the technology from a supporting role to a "pivotal role" on the battlefield.

Equally interesting is what does not feature prominently in Chen’s list of risks. While Framework 3.0 (see below) emphasizes the risk of autonomous systems exceeding their assigned tasks or escaping human control, Chen focuses on how people, states, and hostile actors use AI—and on the risks posed by technological lag. This reflects the concept of “holistic national security,” which views technology as a force multiplier for existing threats and as another arena of competition between states. Accordingly, Chen defines innovation as the "primary driving force" and security as the "bottom-line requirement," calling for the reinforcement of self-reliant AI capabilities alongside mechanisms for monitoring, early warning, and oversight.

Framework 3.0 was developed under the guidance of the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) and organized by the National Cybersecurity Standardization Technical Committee (TC260), in collaboration with research institutes, professional bodies, and technology companies. The institutional response is distributed among several entities: the CAC leads regulation in the areas of services, content, algorithms, and data; TC260 handles standardization and technical tools; and the Ministry of State Security brings a national security perspective. AI providers are responsible for implementing the safety requirements, under the supervision of the relevant regulators.

This is the third version of the framework, which has been updated annually since September 2024. It is not a binding law or regulation, but rather a guiding document built around three tiers: mapping and classifying risks, using technological measures to reduce them, and establishing oversight and governance mechanisms. Among other things, the framework recommends risk assessments, monitoring and early warnings, restricting the permissions of AI agents, human involvement in high-risk operations, audits of tools and plug-ins, and mechanisms for shutting down systems that exceed their assigned tasks. One of the system's guiding principles is promoting AI development while ensuring it remains "safe and controllable" (安全可控).

The framework operates alongside a binding regulatory system that has evolved in China in recent years. This includes rules for generative AI services, registration and review procedures for services and algorithms, and requirements for labeling AI-generated content. As of late August 2026, over one thousand generative AI services have completed the national-level registration process in China. Framework 3.0 provides a risk roadmap and technical principles to guide the further development of standards and regulation, while legal obligations remain anchored in the existing regulatory system.

According to an analysis by AI Safety in China, an independent research project tracking AI policy and governance in China, the number of risks detailed in the framework grew from 30 in Version 2.0 to 54 in Version 3.0. Particular attention is given to AI agents, which can plan, perform tasks, and operate in external systems, and to embodied AI, in which a digital failure could cause physical harm. The framework also addresses systems that obtain unauthorized permissions or resources, deceive safety evaluators, deviate from their intended goal, or act autonomously in cyberspace. In commentary published following the framework's presentation, this change was described as a shift in large models from "answering questions" to "executing tasks."
